Q: Why is the build of my C# project producing the following output during compilation? A:

You are mixing two things here: nuget configuration files *.Config and nuget package feeds (aka sources).

What you (think you) want - configuration files

According to How settings are applied

Multiple NuGet.Config files allow you to store settings in different locations so that they apply to a single solution, or a group of solutions. These settings collectively apply to any NuGet operation invoked from the command line or from Visual Studio

[...]

Specifically, when a config file is not specified explicitly on the command line, NuGet loads settings from the different config files in the following order:

  1. (Uncommon) The NuGetDefaults.Config file, which contains settings related only to package sources.
  2. The computer-level file. [%ProgramFiles(x86)%\NuGet\Config]
  3. The user-level file. [%appdata%\NuGet\NuGet.Config]
  4. Files found in every folder in the path from the drive root to the current folder (where nuget.exe is invoked or the folder containing the Visual Studio solution). For example, if a command is invoked in c:\A\B\C, NuGet looks for and loads config files in c:\, then c:\A, then c:\A\B, and finally c:\A\B\C.

During installation of DevExpress, C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NuGet\\Config\\DevExpress 24.2.config is created. This makes it convenient to use DevExpress in any project, because the nuget configuration for it is always included.

A naive solution for your problem could be to remove that file either by deleting it or moving it to some other folder that's not part of the search hierarchy. However, you'd then have to explicitly add that configuration for every project that uses DevExpress.

What you need - package sources

Due to this aggregation of *.Config files it is somewhat finicky to remove an individual one or it would make other projects more complicated to configure.

Instead, simply accept that C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NuGet\\Config\\DevExpress 24.2.config is always included, just like C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NuGet\\Config\\Microsoft.VisualStudio.Offline.config, even though a particular project might not need anything they do.

Usually, the only "problematic" thing that a *.Config does (in the global context) is that it adds package sources. Now with possibly dozens of aggregated *.Config files, each of them adding possibly dozens of sources, the total number of feeds that should be checked can get very long. In a project that does not use DevExpress you might be asking yourself: "But why does it waste time trying to find every package in the DevExpress nuget feed, even though the project doesn't use anything from that feed?"

Instead of trying to remove the *.Config file, you can limit the nuget sources that are evaluated at the project level. There are multiple ways to do this.

<clear /> 👎

You can add this to any *.Config to essentially "break the chain" of aggregated imports. This is a nuclear option that removes DevExpress 24.2.config, but it also removes everything else from the hierarchy previously defined, like Microsoft.VisualStudio.Offline.config. If you have other *.Config files at the computer-level folder %ProgramFiles(x86)%\NuGet\Config, those would be excluded as well. This option has similar drawbacks to moving DevExpress 24.2.config to a different location.

disable the DevExpress source 👍

This is what AI suggested you to do:

<disabledPackageSources>  
  <add key="DevExpress 24.2 Local" value="true" />  
  <add key="DevExpress_24.2" value="true" />  
</disabledPackageSources>

I did that, but the mentioned line gets back in the output log.

I hope I could make it clear in this answer that your expectation was somewhat mixed up: when you are removing the package sources (that are added though DevExpress 24.2.config), that does not mean that the configuration file DevExpress 24.2.config itself is not considered anymore. Removing the configuration file itself is not really necessary.

To validate if the suggested snippet works, use dotnet nuget list source to list all package sources or try to restore a DevExpress package, which should fail.

The problem of this solution is that you have to explicitly add it to every project that doesn't use DevExpress.

package source mapping 🚀

The no-compromise solution would be to somehow have DevExpress 24.2.config always included by default, for convenience in projects that need it and at the same time somehow ignore the nuget sources that it adds, for projects that don't need them.

This solution comes in the form of Package Source Mapping.

With Package Source Mapping, you can filter, per package, which source(s) NuGet will search.

This is what AI also hinted at:

<packageSourceMapping>  
  <packageSource key="OwnNugetPackagesFeed">  
    <package pattern="Own.\*" />  
  </packageSource>  
  <packageSource key="nuget.org">  
    <package pattern="\*" />  
  </packageSource>  
</packageSourceMapping>

You should be able to limit the DevExpress source to be only searched for DevExpress packages with something like this:

<packageSourceMapping>  
  <packageSource key="DevExpress 24.2 Local">  
    <package pattern="DevExpress.*" />  
  </packageSource>  
</packageSourceMapping>

I'm not a DevExpress user myself and would encourage you to check the file content of DevExpress 24.2.config, because it might already do that for you, which would mean that you don't have to do anything at all.

Q: How to avoid heredoc expanding variables? A:

Just use 'EOF' to prevent the variable from expanding:

sudo /bin/su -c "cat << 'EOF' > /etc/init.d/my-script
#                       ^   ^
... contents go here
EOF

From man bash:

Here Documents

This type of redirection instructs the shell to read input from the current source until a line containing only delimiter (with no trailing blanks) is seen. All of the lines read up to that point are then used as the standard input for a command.

The format of here-documents is:

      <<[-]word
              here-document
      delimiter

No parameter expansion, command substitution, arithmetic expansion, or pathname expansion is performed on word. If any characters in word are quoted, the delimiter is the result of quote removal on word, and the lines in the here-document are not expanded. If word is unquoted, all lines of the here-document are subjected to parameter expansion, command substitution, and arithmetic expansion. In the latter case, the character sequence \<newline> is ignored, and \ must be used to quote the characters \, $, and `.

Q: HTML5 equivalent to <font>? A:

I would maybe question the main motivation of "getting rid of the deprecated markup" in some "locally archived" material: as we can see, doing semi-smart replace of <font size=1..7> to <span style=font-size:xx-small..xxx-large> would very likely fulfil the "modern valid markup" request, without compromising the pixel-perfect rendered outcome (kudos for fellow commenters here for bringing this fact up along the specs and links)… but, is it really worth it?

Even in the current form, "deprecated" from the HTML living standard's perspective, I am pretty confident that no modern browser would dare to effectively remove support for that old <font size="…"> markup during our lifespans. So, keeping the document as-is, seems pretty safe to me to begin with.

(I understand urge to polish code and make individual positive contribution to it, but pragmatically, there is really no objective urge for this endeavour, since it is not going to stop working in any major browser in a foreseeable future. And, probably "never": what browser would dare to blatantly break the backwards compatibility of such basic markup likely present in myriads [1] of historical web content? So unless you have some other plans maintaining and expanding it, I'd simply preserve the "dated" document verbatim with all "deprecated" constructs as an artifact from the dawn of the HTML.)

[1] HTTP Archive 2024: more than 4 % of analysed pages contained <font>
